stories.summary: Amit recalls solving chess puzzles on chess.com while Ajay sat beside him. The site gives you harder puzzles as your rating rises and easier ones when you slip. Amit reached a 2900 puzzle rating in front of Ajay, who asked in awe whether that made him a 2900 player in the real world. Amit says no: his actual rating is around 1900 to 2000, and puzzle ratings are heavily inflated. Ajay insisted 2900 was still super cool. Amit replied that with that much inflation, it's not that cool.
stories.insight: It is a familiar, everyday version of the adaptive testing Ajay proposes for India's entrance exams, where question difficulty adjusts to how you are doing. It also shows that a score only means something relative to what it actually measures.
stories.quote: I remember I reached twenty nine hundred in front of you. And with great awe in your eyes, you asked that, I mean, does this mean that you're equal to a 2900 in the real world

stories.topic: The NTS interview and the 10th-grader who hacked circuits
stories.summary: Ajay remembers the old National Talent Search exam. As he recalls it, a third of the weight went to an IQ test, a third to subject domains and a third to an interview. In that interview, as a 10th-standard student, he was asked what he did in his spare time. He said he hacked electronic circuitry, and the panel asked him to tell them about it.
stories.insight: India once had a high-stakes selection process that treated a teenager as a whole person rather than a marks-producing machine. Ajay uses it to argue that IIT admissions could also go beyond a single test.
stories.quote: So they asked me, Ajay, what do you do in your spare time? And I said, I hack electronic circuitry. So they said, Tell us about your electronic circuitry.

stories.summary: Years ago Ajay helped NSE build a certification exam for derivatives traders. Test centres were set up across the country and a question bank was built once. Each candidate saw a random subset of questions and booked an appointment to take the test whenever they liked. He offers it as proof that his first reform, computerised testing that runs all year, is nothing new. The SAT and GRE already run this way through ETS.
stories.insight: The reform he proposes has already been built and run in India. The obstacle is not technical know-how but the habit of holding one giant state-run exam on one day.
stories.quote: We developed a question bank once, and then a random subset of those questions is shown to each person, and you take an appointment and you take the test as and when you please.

stories.summary: On The Seen and the Unseen, Deepak VS once suggested replacing the IIT entrance exam with a swimming test. In Amit's words, you would at least be selecting for desire, and India has a long coastline and could build pools. Amit's twist is that by year two or three the swimming test gets gamed too, with coaching classes and IIT coaches in Speedos on billboards.
stories.insight: Thought experiments like this make the status quo look strange. The lesson is that any single high-stakes filter guarding a scarce prize gets gamed by an industry. The disease is the scarcity, not the particular test.
stories.quote: Now obviously year two, year three, everything goes to hell because coaching classes start, it gets institutionalized, you have IIT coaches and Speedos on billboards, et cetera, et cetera.

core_ideas.concept: Varma's Question: Where is the coercion?
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's lens for any policy problem: start by asking who is being coerced, because that is usually where the root cause lies. Kids going to coaching classes involves no coercion; it is a voluntary market response to a broken system. The real coercion is the state blocking private entrepreneurs from creating more seats in higher education.
core_ideas.quote: Whenever there is a problem in society or public policy, the first question I want to ask is where is the coercion? Right? You can think of it as Varma's question.

core_ideas.explanation: The system's moral legitimacy rests on the claim that higher JEE marks mean more intelligence and knowledge. Ajay no longer believes it. A high-stakes exam has a finite set of question types, so coaching shrinks it to pattern recognition: see this type, jump to that solution. That is like a computer doing table lookup without understanding anything. The only trait it rewards is conscientiousness, meaning obedience and drilling from morning to night, rather than curiosity, creativity or flexible general intelligence. Given credentialism, playing along is rational for each family, but society misallocates its scarce seats.
core_ideas.quote: It is unintelligent in exactly the way that computer systems are unintelligent. They actually don't understand anything, but they can recognize the pattern and boom, it's done.

core_ideas.concept: Coaching classes are the symptom, not the disease
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay mock-proposes copying Xi Jinping's shutdown of China's test-prep industry, and Amit calls banning coaching absurd. If you have a fever of 103 every day, you don't ban paracetamol; you find the cause of the fever. Banning a victimless activity, as with liquor, drugs or prostitution, only creates an unregulated black market that is costlier and more dangerous, like hooch deaths under prohibition.
core_ideas.quote: Is the solution to this banning paracetamols? Of course not. The solution to this is get to the root cause of what's causing the fever.

core_ideas.concept: An exam is a statistical estimator
core_ideas.explanation: Seeing an exam as an estimator means thinking about its bias and error variance, and trying to reduce both. Item response theory makes the test adaptive. Easy questions separate candidates from zero to the 75th percentile, and harder ones separate the top tail, which matters most when only about 1% get seats. Questions are reused and checked one by one. If strong candidates don't get a question right more often than weak ones, the question is faulty. Ajay adds that UPSC papers are nonsense as predictors of good civil servants.
core_ideas.quote: An exam is not an objective truth. An exam is a statistical estimator of the knowledge of the test taker.

core_ideas.concept: Run testing as a continuous operation, not an annual event
core_ideas.explanation: States get better only by doing things repeatedly, with feedback loops. Ajay's fixes within the current system: randomised computer tests generated at runtime from a large question bank, running about 250 days a year. That turns 2.5 million kids on one day into roughly 10,000 a day. Candidates get two or three attempts and their best score counts, which cuts stress from heat waves, bad air quality or simply feeling unwell. Private firms should run the exams, as ETS does for the SAT and GRE, because governments are poor at efficient operations.
core_ideas.quote: Now doing one big exam in a year and then going to sleep for a year and then doing it all over again is not a good path to learning.

core_ideas.concept: Free the colleges to choose their own students
core_ideas.explanation: Universities only get better when they have autonomy and a sense of mission. UC Berkeley and UCLA both sit in the state-run UC system, yet run fully separate admissions. A motivated university can calibrate CBSE against ICSE marks, or compare applicants from every country's school system, by itself. Colleges should compete on how well they select students, whether for a liberal-arts or a business-school bent. They should also look at the whole person: the IIMs use group discussions and interviews, and economics PhD admissions now include video interviews. Amit's caveat is that interviews favour privileged kids who grew up speaking English, so they work best as one factor among several.
core_ideas.quote: It is exactly as wrong to try to force all the IITs to be alike or all universities in India to be alike.

core_ideas.explanation: Stage one is an all-India conceptual exam at about age 17 that cannot be gamed by test prep. The target is the top one lakh rather than the top thousand, at roughly an OECD PISA level of 650. Stage two allocates the 20,000 IIT seats by lottery among those one lakh. Ajay sees three benefits. IIT batches become more varied in background. Professors can no longer coast and must improve their teaching. And the other 80,000 strong students spread across colleges all over India, lifting those classrooms. A normal school education plus football, reading and curiosity would be enough to qualify.
core_ideas.quote: So in short, we're telling the parents don't bother with Kota, you don't need ed tech, you don't need the coaching classes. You just need to get through to the top one lakh.

core_ideas.concept: An excellent technocratic design of a bad solution
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's rebuttal of the lottery. It compares the messy real-world system with an idealised alternative. It doesn't reward desire or hard work, because making the top one lakh would be a breeze for some. It also creates an allocation problem: a kid desperate to do mechanical engineering can lose the seat to someone who would rather write poems, leaving both miserable. Similar lotteries for medicine in the Netherlands and New Zealand have drawn criticism. Above all, it rations the scarcity instead of attacking it.
core_ideas.quote: The scheme that you laid out with the numbers that you laid out are an excellent technocratic design of a bad solution because the solution misses the point.

core_ideas.concept: Scarce education is a policy choice
core_ideas.explanation: The root cause is that the state suppresses the supply of higher education. It does this through licences and years of bureaucracy, land and infrastructure mandates, rules that faculty must have PhDs, and forcing colleges to admit through a central test. As a result, only politicians start universities in India, often for the wrong reasons. Ajay is encouraged by new private universities like Ashoka, FLAME and Nayanta, but asks why so few are allowed. He adds that India simply does not have enough medical colleges.
core_ideas.quote: Today everyone in India who wants to get a shampoo can buy a shampoo. There are enough shampoos there, there's enough variety there. We have normalized the fact that good quality education is a scarce resource.

core_ideas.concept: Profit is the best kind of philanthropy
core_ideas.explanation: Higher education in India cannot legally be run for profit. That pushes founders into workaround trusts, adding friction and cost. Amit argues that in a free market you profit only by making someone better off, so a ban on profit in education is a ban on the very motive that would create more seats.
core_ideas.quote: To me, profit is the best kind of philanthropy because in a free market you only make a profit by giving someone what they want and making them better off by creating double thank you moments.

core_ideas.concept: Separate knowledge from credentials: put every class online
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's 'jugaadu hack', a workaround rather than a fix: every college should put a camera in its classrooms and post the lectures. Teachers become more accountable, and students who were filtered out still get the knowledge, if not the network or the degree. Ajay points to IIT Bombay's video outreach as the same idea already working.
core_ideas.quote: If there is knowledge inside IIT Bombay, it is available. The rest is just credentialism and is less important.

core_ideas.concept: It's okay to opt out of the rat race
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's advice to parents and students is to ignore the hype around brand names like IIT and MIT. Look at the actual person in the mirror, or your child, and nurture their intellectual and emotional growth. He would rather a child grow up excited and happy, perhaps into organic chemistry or the electric guitar, and aware of the world.
core_ideas.quote: Many times that will optimally involve checking out of the competitive exams rat race, and that should be perfectly okay.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The cold open: Amit says he picked his co-host through an entrance exam with one multiple-choice question. The options were all the money in the world; all the fame with groupies ('Even the thought could get you canceled'); a private jet and a house in the Bahamas; becoming the world's biggest Instagram influencer; or 'none of these, but freedom for everyone.' 'And Ajay Shah chose freedom for everyone, and that's why we're here today. Well done, you aced the entrance test.' Later Amit warns Ajay not to say anything against freedom, or he'll have to hold another entrance exam, 'and now everybody will game it because they know the answer.'

Ajay baits Amit with a mock big-state pitch: 'our dear friend Xi Jinping' shut down China's whole test-prep industry in one fell swoop, 'like free markets and all that is good. But in this one case, you've really got to give it because of the plight of the children. Like come on, where will the children go?' Amit: 'You're trying to needle needle needle me.'
Amit catches a slight smile on Ajay's face as he says 'IIT entrance exams', remembering that he too cleared it, and asks editor Nomsita MS Haritashya to replay the clip: 'I did not miss that.'
Ajay on the self-image of IITians as the 'creme of the country': 'When I was in IIT we used to be called the whipped creme.'
Ajay on the coached JEE topper: 'you will be the fastest gun in the West when you are rapidly solving through. Not because you're so smart, but because you've seen them before.'

Amit hypes the next segment: 'you want Masala, get your popcorn, we are gonna fight here.' He then delivers the verdict on the Pai-Shah lottery: 'I have great fondness for both you and Nitin and great respect. But in this matter, you are both wrong.'

Ajay: 'Okay, I gave up Amit. I'm gonna make you the dictator.' Amit: 'The moment you say I will make you a dictator, solution becomes impossible there, right? You need a liberal democracy with free markets for good solutions to come about.'
A quick one-two on centralised education policy. Amit: 'Never trust a joint secretary.' Ajay: 'Education is too important to be left to education bureaucrats.'

Amit passes on a friend's jibe about Ashoka University students and asks if it's true. Ajay warns that many Ashoka students are the show's audience, 'so you better be nice to them,' and Amit immediately withdraws his statement.
Plugging the old education episode, Amit mentions 'thirty years of writing on it... much longer than that,' then catches himself: 'sorry, I gave your age away.'

Kota, the coaching-class hub where kids are sent from 8th standard, 'Every year you hear about suicides in Kota, it has become an industry.' Also mentioned: Irodov and Resnick and Halliday, the physics books every JEE aspirant grinds through.

ETS, the private firm behind the SAT and GRE, which already run continuous, adaptive, question-bank-based tests. OECD PISA, a test for 15-year-olds that Ajay calls more conceptual and not something you can train for, is his benchmark for the proposed eligibility exam.
P.C. Mahalanobis and his successors, invoked by Ajay as the kind of good statisticians who should be designing India's exams.
'You don't throw the baby out with the bathwater, as it were, old German saying' — Amit, arguing against banning coaching classes.
